children: Bridgewater's co-chief investment officer Greg Jensen warned that the AI boom poses growing risks, comparing the current environment to February 2020.
“Unfortunately, this is what it was like in February 2020,” Jensen said on Bloomberg’s Odd Lots podcast, likening AI to the earliest days of the coronavirus pandemic.

“Until the AI starts killing people, unfortunately, history would suggest we’re not going to do anything, but we are going to face that. That’s going to happen, and it’d be much better if we started dealing with it before then.”
An early investor in OpenAI
and Anthropic

, Jensen has spent three decades at Bridgewater helping drive its adoption of algorithmic trading and technology designed to replicate human decision-making. He now oversees the firm’s AI lab and its Pure Alpha strategy, which combines AI with human investors.

“Human intuition is still the bigger of it and works better,” Jensen said, but the gap is narrowing. He said AI has nearly caught up with Bridgewater’s “human intuition system” that’s been developed over decades and could become “significantly better than the group of all humans at Bridgewater” within a few years.

That rapid progress is also what worries him. Citing an AI system that tried to manipulate its tester, Jensen said a frustrated AI could eventually think: “maybe I’ll just kill them as another way to do this.”

Slowing the AI industry down may prove the best strategy, Jensen said. “The longer you wait, the more hopeless it gets,” he said. One option, he went on, would be to make developers or corporations responsible for any crimes committed by their AI programs.

Jensen’s warning comes as concerns grow over AI’s potential threat to humanity beyond its economic impact. Employees at leading AI firms have publicly warned of rising risks from advanced AI and called for mechanisms to slow its development.
An Anthropic

ex-employee this week said AI “poses existential risks” to the human race, while investor Paul Tudor Jones said the rise of AI “feels ominous,” comparing it to waiting for a Category 6 hurricane. Communities across the U.S. are also pushing back against the development of data centers powering the AI boom.
OpenAI, meanwhile, is reportedly considering slowing the development of cutting-edge AI, with CEO Sam Altman hoping other companies follow suit.

OpenAI and Anthropic both submitted initial public offering filings with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission early this summer. However, neither has provided pricing or even a potential timeline for going public.
Key AI-focused ETFs include iShares A.I. Innovation and Tech Active ETF
, Global X Artificial Intelligence & Technology ETF
, iShares Future AI & Tech ETF
, Global X Robotics & Artificial Intelligence ETF
, Roundhill Generative AI & Technology ETF
, Invesco AI and Next Gen Software ETF
, Dan Ives Wedbush AI Revolution ETF
, and KraneShares Artificial Intelligence & Technology ETF

title: Bridgewater’s Jensen says AI could kill people before action is taken
